result.summary: Pindar invokes the three Graces of Orchomenos, praising them as givers of all pleasant things and honour. He announces the Olympic victory of the boy Asopichos and sends Echo to the underworld to tell his dead father the news.

scenes.title: Editorial note on the ode
scenes.summary: A note explains how the ode was performed and dates the victory to 476 B.C.

scenes.title: Hymn to the Graces
scenes.summary: Pindar prays to the Graces of Orchomenos, praises their power over gods and men, and announces Asopichos's Olympic victory.

scenes.title: Echo sent to the dead father
scenes.summary: Echo is told to fly to Persephone's home and tell Asopichos's father of his son's crown at Pisa.

alias_notes.explanation: Title for the chief god, whom the text does not name here.

notable_quotes.reason: Sums up the Graces' role as source of all pleasant things, wisdom, beauty and fame.
Memorable image of Echo carrying news of victory to the dead.

analysis.text: Victory and beauty are presented as gifts of divine grace, not merely human effort.
The ode celebrates a boy victor in 476 B.C. and was sung by a chorus at Orchomenos, home of the Graces' cult.

fun_facts.text: This is one of Pindar's shortest odes, and its closing message to the dead is among his most admired passages.

language_notes.text: The Minyai were the legendary ancestral people of Orchomenos in Boeotia, said to descend from King Minyas; the city is named as their home.
"Yea even gods... rule never at feast or dance" means the gods cannot order their feasts and dances without the Graces' help.
"Lydian mood" refers to the Lydian mode, a musical scale thought suited to gentle, festive songs.
Persephone's home is the underworld, so the father is dead; Echo is asked to carry news to him there.

context_notes.text: The Kephisos is a river of Boeotia flowing near Orchomenos; the city was famous for its horses and for its cult of the Graces.
Pisa is the district of Olympia, where the Olympic games were held. Victors were crowned with wild olive garlands.

literary_notes.text: The poet addresses the Graces directly as if present, opening the ode as a prayer and setting its reverent tone.
Echo is treated as a messenger who can travel to the dead, turning a natural sound into a link between son and father.
